semantic_correction.stem: A client in the continental United States asks when solar ultraviolet (UV) rays tend to be strongest during daylight saving time. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.B: Mainly during the hour after sunrise.
options.C: Primarily after 6 p.m. on summer days.
options.D: UV intensity remains about the same throughout daylight hours.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC skin-cancer prevention guidance updated February 10, 2026 states that in the continental United States, UV rays are strongest from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. during daylight saving time and from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. during standard time. CDC also notes that UV exposure occurs on cloudy and cool days, so cloud cover does not eliminate the need for sun protection. Therefore option A is correct.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach clients when solar UV exposure tends to be strongest and reinforce that UV exposure is not limited to cloudless conditions.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Reducing Risk for Skin Cancer; Sun Safety Facts
semantic_correction.source_locator: Practice sun safety / Overview — in the continental United States, UV rays are strongest from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. daylight saving time and 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. standard time; UV rays can reach people on cloudy and cool days
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: CDC states that solar UV rays in the continental United States are strongest from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. during daylight saving time and that UV exposure can occur on cloudy and cool days.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed repeated 'only' distractor wording and punctuation cueing, preserved the CDC 10 a.m.–4 p.m. daylight-saving interval, and balanced all choices as time-of-day statements.

audit_findings_append.source_locator: February 10, 2026 skin-cancer prevention and sun-safety guidance
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — sun-safety education
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item directly tests the current CDC peak-UV interval without absolute-word or punctuation cues.

option_audit.A: Correct. It matches the CDC daylight-saving peak-UV interval for the continental United States.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. CDC identifies the midday period rather than just after sunrise as the strongest interval.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. CDC identifies 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., not evening hours, as the peak interval during daylight saving time.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. UV intensity varies with time of day and is strongest around midday.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone matches the CDC time window specified in the stem.
cueing_check: All four options are punctuated time-of-day statements of comparable brevity; no absolute wording or formatting cue identifies A.
